Name: St Martin's Church, Dorking
Short_Description: A church has stood at the heart of Dorking since at least 1086, and the parish traces worship here to Saxon times. The present Grade II*-listed building, rebuilt by Henry Woodyer from 1866 and crowned in 1877 by a 210-foot tower and spire, is a landmark for many miles.
History_or_Lore: A church in Dorking is first recorded in Domesday Book (1086). The parish describes a Saxon church rebuilt in the mid-twelfth century as a cruciform building with a central tower; aisles were added in the fourteenth century. A great wooden pulpit was set centrally in 1637; later in that century the chancel was partitioned off and the transepts used as schoolrooms. By the early nineteenth century the medieval church was dilapidated and too small, and by 1837 the nave had been replaced by a galleried “Intermediate Church,” soon out of favour. Henry Woodyer rebuilt the chancel in 1866–68, the nave and aisles in 1872–74, and completed the west tower and spire in 1877 as the “Wilberforce Memorial,” after Bishop Samuel Wilberforce, who had laid the foundation stone on 29 May 1873, was killed in a riding fall less than two months later. The top stone went on on 25 April 1877; the height to the weather vane, a Dorking cockerel, is 210 feet. The Lady Chapel was added in 1905–13. Historic England lists the church at Grade II*. The south porch holds a 1961 bronze by David McFall to Ralph Vaughan Williams, who grew up at nearby Leith Hill Place.

Name: St Paul's Church, Dorking
Short_Description: Built in 1857 to designs by Benjamin Ferrey, this Grade II-listed flint church was raised among the new streets of Victorian Dorking as an evangelical parish church for a growing railway town.
History_or_Lore: St Paul’s was consecrated in 1857, at first little more than the present nave, on land given by Henry Thomas Hope of The Deepdene. The cost was met by John Labouchere of Broome Hall, Coldharbour, an evangelical banker who also funded the church there; the official list entry names the donor as Henry Labouchere, almost certainly a slip for John. From the outset it was an evangelical church, designed by Benjamin Ferrey in an Early Decorated manner, of flint with stone dressings and a shingled bellcote. As the congregation grew, a north aisle was added in 1860, a south aisle in 1869, a vestry and organ chamber in 1897, and the west porch in 1931. Historic England listed the church at Grade II in 2002. The font was given in 1903 by Lily, Duchess of Marlborough, then of Deepdene. Among the windows is one commemorating Hope, and another to Richard Attlee, a first churchwarden and grandfather of the later prime minister Clement Attlee. The war memorial includes Valentine (Joe) Strudwick, a pupil of St Paul’s School, who enlisted at fourteen and was killed in Belgium aged fifteen, one of the youngest British soldiers to die in the First World War.
Address: St Paul's Road West, Dorking, Surrey RH4 2HT

Name: St Mary the Virgin, Pixham
Short_Description: A Grade II*-listed chapel of ease of 1903, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and paid for by the local benefactor Mary Mayo, this small roughcast church stands on Pixham Lane at the edge of Dorking.
History_or_Lore: St Mary’s is a daughter church of St Martin’s, Dorking, built as a chapel of ease for the hamlet of Pixham. The official list entry dates the building to 1901 and its dedication to 1903; the parish and most architectural accounts give 1903. Lutyens designed a modest but highly original church, roughcast, with brick lacing courses, a steep tiled roof, a western bell-cote and an apse under a continuous roofline. The interior was deliberately dual-purpose: a curtain could screen off the sanctuary when the tunnel-vaulted white nave was used as a clubroom or nursery. The sanctuary, in contrast, has a beautifully proportioned dome on a square base, patterned in chalk, tiles and sandstone, in what Pevsner’s revisers call a sweeter version of Bentley’s Westminster Cathedral style. A nave fireplace has an arched overmantel inscribed as a memorial to the founder’s brothers. Historic England listed the church in 1973 and later raised it to Grade II*. There is no churchyard; burials belonged to the mother parish. No ghost story is firmly attached to the building; its romance lies in the Lutyens invention itself, and in Mayo’s gift of a village church that could also serve as a hall.

Name: St Barnabas Church, Ranmore
Short_Description: Built in 1859 by Sir George Gilbert Scott as the estate church of Denbies, this Grade II*-listed flint church on Ranmore Common, with its tall octagonal spire, has long been known as “the Church on the North Downs Way.”
History_or_Lore: Scott designed St Barnabas for his friend George Cubitt, later first Lord Ashcombe and son of the builder Thomas Cubitt, and was a frequent visitor to nearby Denbies, the family house demolished in 1954. The church is cruciform, of flint cobbles with ashlar dressings, with a large central octagonal tower and a tall facetted spire. The interior is richly finished in coloured marble and alabaster. One unusual feature, noted by the National Churches Trust, is that the main door faces away from the road, because the church was designed to be entered from the Great House. The south transept became a memorial chapel, with a war memorial erected in 1920 by the second Baron Ashcombe for his three sons killed in the First World War, and painted by the late Pre-Raphaelite artist Reginald Frampton. A vestry was added in 1911. In 1962, after the death of the third Baron, patronage passed to the Church Commissioners and the church was united with St Martin’s, Dorking. First Lord Ashcombe is buried east of the chancel. A former Bishop of Guildford, visiting, called it “my other cathedral in the woods.” Most services still follow the 1662 Book of Common Prayer.
Address: Ranmore Common Road, Ranmore Common, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6SP

Name: St James Church, Abinger
Short_Description: The nave of this Grade II*-listed village church is early twelfth-century, and the parish suggests a still older, perhaps wooden, church may once have stood on this high, ancient site beside Abinger Common.
History_or_Lore: A church, perhaps of wood, may have stood here before the Norman Conquest, but nothing of it remains. The site is the third highest of Surrey’s ancient churches. The nave is early twelfth-century; a new chancel and north chapel were built around 1220. In the thirteenth century the church was dedicated to St James, patron saint of pilgrims, and it stands near the old Pilgrims’ Way. The parish recounts that villagers once held churchyard fairs to welcome passing pilgrims; the Old Fair of Abinger, begun in 1956, commemorates those gatherings each June. Restored in 1857 by Henry Goodyer, it was twice struck by disaster. At about 8 a.m. on 3 August 1944, minutes before communion, a flying bomb brought down the belfry, nave roof and parts of the walls; only the thirteenth-century chapel remained largely intact, and no one was hurt. Two bottles of communion wine were found unbroken in the wreckage. Frederick Etchells rebuilt the church, reconsecrated in 1951. A crusader’s stone tomb, found beyond the west wall, was broken up in the works. In June 1964 lightning set the tower on fire, and the church was restored once more. Historic England listed it at Grade II* in 1966.
Address: Abinger Lane, Abinger Common, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6HZ

Name: St John the Evangelist, Wotton
Short_Description: A Grade I-listed village church of Saxon and Norman origin, with a late-seventeenth-century mortuary chapel containing the plain coffin-shaped tombs of the diarist John Evelyn and his wife Mary.
History_or_Lore: The church website traces the building to Saxon times, though only a few original footings now remain to the west of the Norman tower. Historic England, which listed it at Grade I in 1966, describes it as probably of Saxon origin, with mid-eleventh-century Norman nave wall and tower, and thirteenth-century chancel, north chapel, north aisle and nave. The Evelyn Mortuary Chapel on the north is of late seventeenth-century thin brick. Among the monuments are two unornamented coffin-shaped slabs to John Evelyn, 1706, and his wife, 1709. A screen of 1632, noted as one of the few of that period to survive in Surrey, stands between north aisle and chapel. The list entry adds that some churchyard trees were reputedly planted by Evelyn. The church identifies unusual carved heads around the porch door as King John and Archbishop Stephen Langton. No haunting is firmly recorded in the church; the ghost stories belong to nearby Wotton House, once the Evelyn seat. Visit Mole Valley relates that firefighters sent to a blaze there in the 1960s claimed to see a figure carrying fishing gear, and that Bishop Samuel Wilberforce’s ghost may be seen at the house windows on the anniversary of his death.
Address: Church Lane, off Guildford Road (A25), Wotton, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6QQ

Name: Holy Trinity Church, Westcott
Short_Description: Built in 1851–52 to designs by Sir George Gilbert Scott and consecrated in 1852, this Grade II*-listed flint church, with its shingled spire, stands on a hillside above Westcott looking across to Ranmore.
History_or_Lore: Holy Trinity was built on land given by the Evelyn family, lords of the manor of Westcott, when a new parish with a population of about a thousand was taken out of Dorking. The cost was raised by subscription. Charles Barclay of Bury Hill was the principal benefactor; the parish also names Lady Mary Leslie among the original donors. Barclay patronage continued until 1992. Scott designed a fourteenth-century Decorated building of knapped flint, with a timber, shingled spire, seating about 250. The Bishop of Winchester consecrated it in 1852. A south aisle followed in 1855, and Historic England listed the church at Grade II* in 1973. The clock was installed in 1887 for Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee; the lych-gate was added three years later. The outstanding east window, an Ascension by James Powell & Son, was given by Miss Barclay of Rokefield in 1893. Ten windows were destroyed by enemy action in 1940 and replaced with plain leading; two small panels of the lost Leslie Memorial Window survive in the west window. A carved relief of the Happy Warrior, from the studio of G. F. Watts, commemorates Second Lieutenant Boyd Burnet Geake, killed on the Somme in 1916.
Address: Westcott Heath, Westcott, Dorking, Surrey RH4 3JZ

Name: St Michael and All Angels, Mickleham
Short_Description: A Grade II* church of tenth-century origins beside the Mole at Mickleham, with a probably Saxon west door, a late-twelfth-century core and a celebrated Norman font. Fanny Burney was married here in 1793, and Leopold Salomons, who gave Box Hill to the nation, is buried at the church.
History_or_Lore: The parish traces a church on this site first recorded in Domesday Book, and suggests Saxon work as early as about 950; Historic England notes tenth-century origins and a narrow west door, probably of that date. Much of what stands is late twelfth-century: nave, south aisle, chancel and west tower, and the Norbury Chapel of about 1300. P. F. Robinson restored the church in 1823; in 1872 a north aisle was added and most of the fabric, apart from the tower, was largely rebuilt. The Norman chancel arch, raised that year, has chevron and dog-tooth ornament. The font, its basin cut from a single stone, is a fine Norman survival. The Norbury Chapel holds the chest-tomb of William Wyddowson and his wife, dated 1514; it later became the pew of the Locks of Norbury Park, and the outline of their fireplace can still be traced. Oak panelling is said to have been rescued from St Paul’s School in the Great Fire of 1666. Fanny Burney married the émigré General Alexandre d’Arblay here on 28 July 1793, against her father’s wishes. Leopold Salomons, who gave Box Hill to the National Trust, was buried at this church. Grade II*, listed in 1951.
Address: Old London Road, Mickleham, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6DU

Name: St Michael's Church, Betchworth
Short_Description: A Grade I parish church recorded in Domesday Book (1086), with Saxon fragments and a largely medieval fabric, much altered when its Norman crossing tower was moved in 1850–51. It later appeared as the first church in the film Four Weddings and a Funeral.
History_or_Lore: A church at Betchworth is recorded in Domesday Book (1086). Historic England notes Saxon origins, with pre-Conquest fragments, later eleventh-century tower walling, a south aisle of about 1200, and a later thirteenth-century chancel and lady chapel. The medieval parish was unusually large, taking in Brockham as well as Betchworth; the advowson was granted to St Mary Overie, now Southwark Cathedral, in 1199. In 1850–51 the architect E. C. Hakewill demolished the old Norman crossing tower and rebuilt it at the end of the south aisle, resetting a post-Conquest crossing arch and a pre-Conquest capital. The north transept, the Goulburn Chapel, was added in 1879. Historic England listed the church at Grade I in 1966. Among the fittings are a florid polychrome marble pulpit of about 1885 and a tub font of 1951 by Eric Kennington, carved with St Michael and the Madonna. Memorials include those connected with royal surgeons: the family of Thomas Morstede, surgeon at Agincourt, and Sir Benjamin Brodie, surgeon to William IV and Queen Victoria. The parish notes that the church featured as the first church in the film Four Weddings and a Funeral.

Name: St Peter's Church, Newdigate
Short_Description: A Grade II* village church whose earliest dateable work is of about 1200, famous for its weatherboarded timber tower, oak bell-cage and shingled broach spire. Local tradition has sometimes wondered whether it began as a hunters’ chapel in the woods.
History_or_Lore: The earliest firmly dateable work is of about 1200. Local history suggests, as a supposition only, that the church may have begun as a hunters’ chapel serving nobles who used the iron-working woods at Ewood and could not easily return to their palaces the same day. Historic England lists a twelfth- and thirteenth-century church of sandstone rubble, with a fifteenth-century timber belfry; the weatherboarded west tower, with its internal oak bell-cage and shingled broach spire, is the building’s great curiosity. Local accounts date the main timbers to trees felled in 1525, and the list describes a spectacular oak bell-cage with double scissor bracing. Among the oldest fittings is an oak chest with three locks, traditionally used for parish records. By the 1870s the church was dilapidated; T. E. C. Streatfeild restored it in 1876–77, adding a north aisle, vestry and porch, and preserving the ornate 1627 gallery front. The six bells were recast at Whitechapel in 1969. Historic England listed the church at Grade II* in 1966. Visit Mole Valley notes some 800 years of worship here. No ghost story is firmly attached to the church itself.
Address: Church Lane, Newdigate, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5DL

Name: St James Church, Shere
Short_Description: A Grade I Norman church in one of Surrey’s most photographed villages, with worship here dated by the parish to 1190. Its north chancel wall still shows the quatrefoil and squint of Christine Carpenter’s fourteenth-century anchorite’s cell.
History_or_Lore: The parish dates worship here to 1190. Historic England describes a twelfth-century Norman tower and north nave wall, a thirteenth-century south aisle and chapel, a fourteenth-century lengthening and chancel, restored in 1895 by S. Weatherley, and lists the church at Grade I. The broach spire is a fine medieval example, its covering renewed in handmade oak shakes in 2000. In the north wall of the chancel a fourteenth-century quatrefoil and squint mark the site of an anchorite’s cell. In 1329 Christine, daughter of William Carpenter of Shere, received the Bishop of Winchester’s licence to be enclosed there. After about three years she left the cell; on 10 November 1332 the bishop, at her request, agreed to her re-enclosure, that “she may be enabled to achieve her salvation.” The documents survive in Bishop John Stratford’s register. Food was passed through an external grating; through the squint she could see the altar, and through the quatrefoil receive communion. The lych-gate of 1902 is by Edwin Lutyens, who also designed houses in the village for the Bray family, lords of the manor since 1487. The village has often been used as a film location, including The Holiday and Bridget Jones’s Diary.
Address: The Square, Shere, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9HG

Name: Christ Church, Brockham
Short_Description: A Grade II Early English church of 1846–47 by Benjamin Ferrey, built as a memorial to Henry Goulburn the younger on land given by Henry Thomas Hope of Deepdene. It has stood on Brockham Green since its consecration on 12 January 1847.
History_or_Lore: For centuries Brockham people worshipped at St Michael’s, Betchworth. Henry Goulburn the younger, son of the former Chancellor of the Exchequer who had bought the manor of East Betchworth, had long wished for a church on the Green and had begun to collect money for it; he died in 1845, aged thirty, and his father and friends completed the plan as his memorial. Henry Thomas Hope of Deepdene gave the site. The architect was Benjamin Ferrey, a pupil of Pugin. Sir Benjamin Brodie of Broome Park offered all the stone for the walls from his Box Hill quarries, but much of it later proved unsound, and a heavy restoration of 1883 replaced decayed quoins with Bath stone. The Bishop of Winchester consecrated the church on 12 January 1847; it became a separate parish in 1868. Historic England lists it at Grade II. Hope also provided the first clock, which had belonged to Betchworth Castle, dismantled after he bought the park in 1834. The service bell in use today was that clock’s hour bell. A carved wooden reredos of 1885 and an octagonal stone font enrich the interior. The lych-gate of 1931 is by the local architect Frederick Hagyard.
Address: Brockham Green, Brockham, Betchworth, Surrey RH3 7JR

Name: St Mary the Virgin, Buckland
Short_Description: A Grade II village church recorded in Domesday Book (1086), though the present building is thought to date from around 1380 and was remodelled by Henry Woodyer in 1860. Pevsner judged the result “Victorian village church building at its best.”
History_or_Lore: A church at Buckland is recorded in Domesday Book (1086). The parish considers it likely that the Domesday church stood about half a mile away, on Rectory Lane, and that the present building dates from around 1380; the nave walls, the timbers supporting the tower, and two stained-glass windows are believed to be of that period. Historic England lists a fourteenth- and fifteenth-century church, effectively remodelled and rebuilt in 1860 by Henry Woodyer, and graded II in 1966. Woodyer refaced the exterior in ironstone, added a spiral stair to the shingled bellcote, and introduced stained glass by Hardman of Birmingham; fragments of fourteenth-century glass, of St Peter and St Paul, remain in the nave. Pevsner’s Surrey volume calls the result “Victorian village church building at its best.” No ghost is firmly attached to the church itself, but the village has a well-known monster legend: the Buckland Shag, a horse-like creature said once to have dragged travellers from the coach road to devour them in the Shag Brook, whose source is in the village.
Address: Reigate Road (A25), Buckland, Betchworth, Surrey RH3 7BB

Name: St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, Dorking
Short_Description: Dorking’s Roman Catholic parish church, designed by F. A. Walters, with its foundation stone laid on 17 May 1894 and opened the following year on a hillside above the town. The intended tower and some aisles were never built.
History_or_Lore: The Catholic mission in Dorking was firmly established under the Reverend Jean-François Volckeryck, parish priest from 1879 to 1903, a Belgian who, the parish records, could not speak English when he arrived after fifteen years’ ministry in Jersey. In 1888 he arranged the transfer of the hillside site from the Duke of Norfolk to the diocesan trustees. The foundation stone was laid on 17 May 1894; the church, designed by the prolific Catholic architect Frederick A. Walters and financed by the 15th Duke of Norfolk and donations from France and Belgium, was opened in 1895, with the Duke and members of the Howard family present. It is of Bargate or Godalming stone with Bath stone dressings, set high above the town and approached by a dramatic flight of steps. Walters intended a nave with aisles, a south tower and a western baptistery, but the north aisle, south chapel and tower were never built — which, Taking Stock notes, is why the church is not listed, though the completed scheme would have merited it. The presbytery, by Gilbert Blount, predates the church and was built in 1871. Good fittings include a painted reredos and a tapestry of 1993 by Margaret Rohlfing.

Name: Dorking United Reformed Church
Short_Description: A Grade II Congregational church of 1834 on West Street, with a temple-like pedimented façade, serving a dissenting congregation that traces its origins to the ejected clergy of 1662.
History_or_Lore: The congregation traces its origin to 1662, when, under the Act of Uniformity, clergy who would not conform to the Church of England were ejected. The church’s own account records that the founders of what became Dorking Congregational Church began to gather in houses, first at Fetcham and then at North Chapel, before moving in 1695, under the Reverend Samuel Brookes, to a barn on Butter Hill, opposite the Friends Meeting House. A dedicated meeting house was built on West Street in 1719 and replaced in 1834 by the present temple-fronted building. Historic England lists it at Grade II (1973), dating it to 1834, of brick with a stuccoed, pedimented façade of three bays, and naming the architects as William Hopperton of London and Shearburn. In 1972 the Congregational and Presbyterian Churches in England and Wales united to form the United Reformed Church, and the West Street church took that name. It remains a working town-centre church at 153 West Street, a short walk from William Mullins’s house and Dorking Museum.

Name: St John the Baptist, Capel
Short_Description: A Grade II* church whose main fabric was built around 1240, with dog-tooth doorways and a sturdy early nave and chancel. An ancient yew by the churchyard entrance is said to be some 1,700 years old, and local folklore warns against walking round it a hundred times at midnight.
History_or_Lore: The main body of the church was built around 1240, and much of what is seen today belongs to that campaign: the west porch with its unusual rafters, the roof, the west and south doors with dog-tooth mouldings, and the west and south walls of the nave and the east and south walls of the chancel. Historic England lists the church at Grade II*. A restoration of 1864–65 added the churchyard wall and lych-gate. Visit Mole Valley, echoing an older description, calls it a strong example of the hamlet-chapels of the late twelfth or early thirteenth century. Near the churchyard entrance stands an ancient yew, said to be some 1,700 years old, older than the church itself. Local folklore, recorded by Visit Mole Valley, holds that a ghost will appear to anyone who walks around the tree a hundred times at midnight — a tradition the tourist board does not recommend trying. The oldest surviving gravestone in the churchyard is dated 1694.
Address: The Street, Capel, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5JY

Name: Christ Church, Coldharbour
Short_Description: A Grade II hillside church of 1848 by Benjamin Ferrey, of local Leith Hill sandstone, built for John Labouchere of Broome Hall and consecrated on 19 October 1848. Its interior was recast in 1904 by W. D. Caröe, with help from the Vaughan Williams family of nearby Leith Hill Place.
History_or_Lore: Christ Church was built in 1848 to serve a growing hillside village, funded by the evangelical banker John Labouchere of Broome Hall, who also paid for St Paul’s, Dorking, on land given by the 13th Duke of Norfolk. The architect was Benjamin Ferrey, a pupil of Pugin. He designed a simple chapel in a late-thirteenth-century manner, of local Leith Hill sandstone, with Decorated tracery to the chancel arch and windows. The Bishop of Winchester, Charles Sumner, consecrated it on 19 October 1848 as a chapel of ease to Holmwood; Labouchere’s endowment made Coldharbour a parish in its own right in 1850. Historic England lists the church at Grade II. In 1904 Sir Alexander Hargreaves Brown of Broome Hall, the Heaths of Kitlands, and Hervey Vaughan Williams of Leith Hill Place paid for an interior reconstruction by W. D. Caröe, including a new nave roof, choir stalls, reredos and pulpit, and a Rothwell organ; Ralph Vaughan Williams’s sister Margaret paid for a restoration of the organ in 1932. The church has been united with St James’s, Abinger, since 1956. The original 1848 reredos panels, painted with the Commandments, Lord’s Prayer and Creed, now hang on the west gallery.
Address: Abinger Road, Coldharbour, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6HF

Name: St Mary the Virgin, Holmbury St Mary
Short_Description: A Grade I church of 1879, designed, built and given to the parish by the Victorian architect George Edmund Street in memory of his second wife, Jessie. The village itself was renamed Holmbury St Mary after the new church.
History_or_Lore: When the architect George Edmund Street visited the hillside hamlet of Felday in 1872, his first wife, Mariquita, liked it so much that she called it “Heaven’s Gate.” They began to build a house, Holmdale, but she died in 1874 before it was finished. Street remarried in 1876; his second wife, Jessie, fell ill on their honeymoon and died soon afterwards. A devout churchman, he then designed, oversaw and paid for a new parish church in Jessie’s memory, of Holmbury Hill sandstone with Bath stone dressings, completed and consecrated in 1879. Most of the stained glass was also designed by him and made by Clayton & Bell. Historic England lists the church at Grade I. The village of Felday was combined with Pitland Street and renamed Holmbury St Mary after the new church — an unusual case of a village taking its name from its church. Street died in 1881, after a stroke while walking home from Gomshall station; a memorial in the churchyard was designed by his son. Edwin Waterhouse, founder of the accountancy firm, is also buried there.
Address: Horsham Road, Holmbury St Mary, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6PF

Name: St Peter and St Paul (Old Saxon Church), Albury
Short_Description: A Grade I church of Saxon and Norman origin in the parkland of Albury Park, now in the care of the Churches Conservation Trust. Its south transept was remodelled in 1839 by A. W. Pugin as a richly decorated mortuary chapel for the Drummond family.
History_or_Lore: This ancient parish church, of Saxon and Norman origin, stands in the parkland of Albury Park above the Tillingbourne. Among its treasures are a thirteenth-century door, a well-preserved fifteenth-century wall painting of St Christopher, and a brass to John Weston, who died in 1440. In 1819 the banker Henry Drummond bought the estate. The seventeenth-century spire was replaced in 1820 by the present shingled cupola. In the 1830s, as the churchyard filled and the fabric decayed, and after a well-documented rift with his rector, Hugh McNeile, over Drummond’s involvement with the Irvingites, Drummond closed the old church and built a new parish church in the village. Whether that rift decided the closure, the parish site notes, “must remain a matter of conjecture.” The author Martin Tupper led public opposition until the Bishop of Winchester asked him to desist. The closure allowed Drummond, in 1839, to commission the young A. W. Pugin to turn the south transept into a lavishly decorated mortuary chapel for the family, with stained glass, painted walls and ceiling, and a tiled floor. The church is Grade I listed and is now in the care of the Churches Conservation Trust.
Address: Albury Park, Albury, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9BB
